newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian court grants Aboriginal flag copyright.
newsitem.headline: Australian court grants Aboriginal flag copyright.

text.p: An Aboriginal artist won a legal battle on Wednesday to be awarded copyright of the Aboriginal flag, which has become a symbol in Australia for indigenous rights.
A Federal Court judge recognised a claim by Harold Thomas, who lives near Darwin in Australia's north, that he was the designer of the distinctive black, red and yellow flag.

A potent symbol of Aborigines' sruggle to win land rights, the flag was also at the centre of a controversy in 1994 when Aboriginal athlete Cathy Freeman carried it on a victory lap, along with the Australian flag, at the 1994 Commonwealth Games.
Thomas said he designed the flag after an Aboriginal protest march in 1970 when he realised that student and union supporters all had banners, but indigenous people had no flag of their own.
He chose the colours red ochre and yellow ochre because they were dominant in Aboriginal art, and black because it represented "black consciousness, black awareness, black power".
The flag has a red bottom half, representing the earth, a black top half, representing Aboriginal people, and a yellow circle in the centre for the sun.

The judge said Thomas, who was born in 1947 but taken from his parents as a child and raised by a white clergyman and his wife in Adelaide, had not claimed copyright earlier because he was recognised by many Aborigines as the flag's designer.
However, be "bitterly resented" his work being proclaimed in 1995 under the Australian government's Flags Act and described as a flag of significance to the Australian nation.
Thomas and other Aboriginal people believed the flag belonged to the Aboriginal people and not the Australian people as a whole, the judge said.
Thomas's claim was unsuccessfully contested in court by two men, who each said they owned the copyright to the flag's design.
